title: The Inventory of Anderlecht
premise: Sable Halloran, a night librarian in the sleepless city of Anderlecht, has spent eleven years avoiding the grief of his mother's death by cataloguing everything else — books, strangers, his own life reduced to inventory. When a late-night radio station broadcasts a song he knows was written in his mother's kitchen and never recorded, Sable becomes convinced someone is stealing from the past, and his search for the song's source forces him through the city's forgotten rooms, recording studios, and hospice wards. Along the way he befriends Odile, a retired archivist who remembers his mother, and confronts the truth: the song was performed once, illegally, at a protest where a man died, and his mother carried that guilt into silence. In the end, Sable records the song himself in the library after hours and speaks his goodbye aloud to an empty reading room — not recovering his mother's memory, but finally becoming its owner rather than its tenant.
about_author: Ada Sandoval is the pen name of a former hospital archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the belongings of the deceased before turning to fiction. She writes at night, in cities that refuse to sleep, and claims every novel begins as an unrecorded song.

chapters.title: The Night Shift of Small Things
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Sable's POV. We meet Sable shelving returns at the Anderlecht municipal library between midnight and dawn, cataloguing details of patrons' lives he'll never use. He visits his mother's sealed apartment monthly but never enters past the hallway. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as order; the reader feels a man keeping grief on a high shelf.

chapters.title: A Song With No Address
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Driving home at 4 a.m., a pirate radio frequency plays a melody Sable recognizes instantly — one his mother hummed while cooking, a song she claimed she'd written and never recorded. The DJ gives no title or artist. He sits in the parked car until sunrise. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past reaching out and touching him without permission.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Ledger
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, with a flashback to age nineteen. He tries to resume normal life but finds himself auditing his own existence — rent receipts, unread messages, a friendship allowed to lapse. A flashback shows his mother refusing, gently but absolutely, to ever record her songs. Emotional beat: the recognition that avoidance has become his architecture.

chapters.title: Frequency 87.3
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. He stakes out the radio signal nightly, mapping when it plays. The station broadcasts only between 2 and 5 a.m., no call sign, no ads. He leaves a note taped to a transmitter tower on the edge of the Marolles district. Emotional beat: obsession kindling into purpose — the first want he's felt in years.

chapters.title: Odile Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Odile's POV (first time). An eighty-year-old former city archivist receives Sable in her cluttered flat because he traced the transmitter's electricity meter to her building. She recognizes his surname and goes very still. Emotional beat: guarded recognition; two keepers of records circling a shared secret neither will name yet.

chapters.title: What the Kitchen Knew
chapters.summary: Alternating Sable and Odile POVs. Odile confirms the song existed — she heard it once, live, in 1989, in a squatted theater. She refuses to say more. Sable breaks into his mother's apartment for the first time in three years and finds a cassette labeled only with a date. Emotional beat: grief cracking open like a door left unlatched.

chapters.title: The Squatted Theater, 1989
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, extended flashback. The theater nights: musicians, immigrants, students, and a young woman named Marta Halloran singing songs no one was allowed to record because recorded songs could testify. Odile recalls a raid, a fall, a death the police called an accident. Emotional beat: the weight of testimony; memory as contraband.

chapters.title: Evidence of Absence
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. He plays the cassette in the library's listening booth: his mother's voice, younger, mid-song, then a door, shouting, tape hiss. The song cuts off exactly where the radio version continues. Someone finished it. Emotional beat: dread braided with longing; the archive becoming a crime scene.

chapters.title: The Man Who Fell
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She tells Sable about Tomas Verhoeven, the sound engineer who ran the theater's illegal recordings and died in the raid — officially a suicide, actually a push. His mother witnessed it. Her silence wasn't cowardice, Odile insists; it was protection, possibly of Sable himself. Emotional beat: moral vertigo; justice revealed as something the law never touched.

chapters.title: Requests and Dedications
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. He calls into the pirate frequency during open request hours and asks, on air, who is playing Marta Halloran's unfinished song. Dead air, then a voice: 'Come find out.' An address follows. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into resolve; the hunt now knows his name too.

chapters.title: The House of Standing Water
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The address leads to a derelict swimming pool turned rehearsal space, where he meets Jonas, a musician in his sixties who was Tomas's apprentice. Jonas admits he's been broadcasting the song for years, hoping the right person would hear. Emotional beat: confrontation curdling into kinship; two mourners recognizing each other's methods.

chapters.title: Why She Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Jonas's POV, flashback-heavy. Jonas explains: the master tapes of that night contain audio proving the police lieutenant who led the raid killed Tomas — and Marta took the only copy and vanished with it. Recording anything risked drawing the lieutenant's attention back. Emotional beat: the terrible arithmetic of silence; love measured in things withheld.

chapters.title: The Lieutenant Still Lives Here
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Researching old news clippings in his own library, Sable discovers the lieutenant, now retired and decorated, lives twelve streets away and chairs a police benevolent fund. The law closed the case decades ago. Emotional beat: cold fury; the discovery that justice outside the law requires a person willing to carry it.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Mother
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, intimate and slow. He finally empties his mother's apartment, item by item, cataloguing each object honestly for the first time. Behind a radiator: a second cassette, unlabeled, and a letter addressed to him, unopened, dated the week before she died. Emotional beat: tenderness breaking through ritual; the tenant beginning to take possession.

chapters.title: The Letter That Waited Eleven Years
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The letter reveals his mother hid the master tape inside the piano she donated to the library's children's room — and that she chose silence partly to protect Sable, whom the lieutenant had already visited once, asking questions about a boy who might have heard something. Emotional beat: devastation and relief entangled; understanding arriving too late to thank her.

chapters.title: What the Piano Held
chapters.summary: Sable and Odile's POV, alternating. They retrieve the reel from the piano after closing hours. The recording is clear: the lieutenant's voice giving the order, Tomas's last sounds, Marta's breathing behind the camera. Odile weeps for the first time in the book. Emotional beat: proof at last — and the sudden terror of holding something that demands action.

chapters.title: The Weight of Proof
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs — Sable, Odile, Jonas. Debate: give the tape to police (the lieutenant's old colleagues), to journalists (who may bury it), or broadcast it on the pirate frequency where it can't be confiscated. Odile argues memory belongs to everyone or no one. Emotional beat: rising tension; the ethics of vengeance versus witness.

chapters.title: Ninety-Nine Nights of Static
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. They prepare the broadcast over weeks, splicing the tape with his mother's cassette so the song plays complete for the first time since 1989 — testimony embedded in music. The lieutenant's family notices Sable watching their house. Threats arrive, quiet and deniable. Emotional beat: dread climbing toward the peak; no turning back.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax. Multiple POVs converge on the night of transmission. At 3 a.m. the song plays across the city, complete, followed by the raid recording. Listeners call in; old witnesses speak on air; the lieutenant is recognized by name by hundreds. Police trace the transmitter but find only an empty pool and a playing tape loop. Emotional beat: catharsis and exposure; the city forced to remember together.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Unarchived
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The case reopens; the lieutenant, disgraced, dies of a stroke before trial — justice arrives incomplete, which Sable must accept. Jonas donates the original reels to the national archive under Marta's name. Emotional beat: sober reckoning; the difference between resolution and repair.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Out Loud
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. In the empty reading room at dawn, Sable speaks his goodbye aloud — every unsaid thing, eleven years of it — then sings his mother's song badly, completely, alone. He enters her apartment one final time and opens every window. Emotional beat: release; grief transformed from inventory into inheritance.

chapters.title: The Owner's Copy
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Sable's POV, one year later. Sable still works nights but now teaches a memory-oral-history workshop in the library; Odile co-leads it. On the anniversary, the pirate frequency plays the song again, credited to Marta Halloran. Sable signs the library's guest ledger not as staff but as family of the donor. Emotional beat: belonging earned; a tenant become owner of his own past.
